content.title: About
content.content: Beef oxtails are the meat from the tail of a cattle. They are rich in gelatin, have a deep beefy flavor, and become tender and slightly gelatinous after long simmering.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Oxtails are a staple in many world cuisines: French pot-au-feu, American oxtail soup, Asian braised dishes.
The high gelatin content makes oxtail broth thick and flavorful.
In some cultures oxtails are considered a delicacy and are featured in fine‑dining menus.
Slow cooking usually takes 3–4 hours for the meat to fall off the bone.
Beef oxtails provide collagen that turns into gelatin during cooking, beneficial for joints and skin.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Oxtails supply high‑quality animal protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of collagen
items.content: Collagen from gelatin supports joint health, skin elasticity, and hair strength.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Iron from beef helps maintain normal hemoglobin levels and prevents anemia.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Oxtails provide vitamin B12 and niacin, important for energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Calcium, phosphorus and zinc contribute to bone health and immune function.

items.title: High in saturated fat
items.content: Oxtails contain a notable amount of saturated fat, so they should be eaten in moderation.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beef.

items.title: Thorough cooking required
items.content: Undercooked oxtails can harbor harmful bacteria; ensure they are cooked until fully tender.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: Oxtails are high in purines, which may exacerbate gout in susceptible people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Oxtails are typically braised slowly in a broth with vegetables and spices. They can also be roasted, pressure‑cooked, or used in soups and stews. Before cooking, trim excess skin and fat for a cleaner dish.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh oxtails refrigerated at 0–4 °C for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight bag for up to 6 months. Thaw frozen oxtails in the refrigerator before cooking.

content.title: About
content.content: Brick (Brie) is a soft, ripened cheese with a white mold rind, originating from the Île-de-France region of France. It has a mild buttery flavor with subtle mushroom notes and a creamy texture. The cheese is typically aged from 4 to 8 weeks.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brie is often called the “king of cheeses” because of its historic popularity among French aristocracy.
Traditional brick is made from cow’s milk, but goat and sheep milk versions also exist.
The rind forms thanks to the noble mold Penicillium candidum, which gives the cheese its characteristic aroma.
Originally, brick is sold in a round wheel about 30 cm in diameter, though today many smaller portions are available.
There are several varieties such as Brie de Meaux, Brie de Melun, and Brie de Montmartre, each with distinct flavor and aging time.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Brick provides a good amount of calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: The cheese supplies high‑quality animal protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Brick contains vitamins B2, B12 and niacin, supporting energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Probiotics
items.content: Fermentation introduces beneficial bacteria that can promote gut health.

items.title: Low in lactose
items.content: During aging part of the lactose is broken down, making brick often tolerable for people with mild lactose intolerance.

items.title: Milk‑protein allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to casein or whey proteins should avoid brick.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Brick is a high‑fat cheese, so it should be consumed in moderation.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: The cheese can contain a notable amount of salt; those monitoring sodium intake should limit portions.

items.title: Mold sensitivity
items.content: While Penicillium candidum is safe, people with weakened immune systems or mold sensitivities should be cautious.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve brick at room temperature, sliced or cut into wedges. It pairs well with bread, crackers, fruits (pear, apple) and nuts. The cheese complements red wines and certain beers. In cooking, brick is used in sauces, casseroles and on pizza.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep brick in its original packaging or wrapped in parchment placed inside an airtight container in the refrigerator at 2‑4 °C. Consume within 1‑2 weeks after opening. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or any mold other than the white rind.

double-hamburger-on-wheat-bun-2-medium-p.title: Double Hamburger on Wheat Bun, 2 Medium Patties

content.title: About
content.content: The double hamburger consists of a wheat bun, two medium beef patties (about 100 g each), lettuce, a slice of tomato, cheese, pickles and sauce. It is a classic fast‑food item popular worldwide.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first double hamburger appeared in the United States in the 1970s as a larger version of the classic burger.
A wheat bun gives a softer texture compared to the traditional white‑bread bun.
Two patties increase the protein content to about 40 g per serving.
The burger is often served as a combo with fries and a soft drink.
Some restaurants use beef raised without hormones for the patties.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: Two patties provide roughly 40 g of protein, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Iron and zinc
items.content: Beef is rich in iron and zinc, essential for immune function and metabolism.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The patties contain vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, which aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Fiber from vegetables
items.content: Lettuce, tomato and pickles add dietary fiber that benefits digestion.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: The burger quickly replenishes energy through a balance of protein, fat and carbohydrates.

items.title: High calories and saturated fat
items.content: A double hamburger can contain over 800 kcal and a notable amount of saturated fat.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Sauces and processed ingredients increase salt levels, which may be an issue for hypertension.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The wheat bun contains gluten, unsuitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Potential additives
items.content: Some establishments use preservatives and flavor enhancers that can cause reactions in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the burger hot. Eat it with your hands, adding ketchup, mustard or mayo to taste. For a healthier option, swap the bun for a whole‑grain version and load up on extra fresh vegetables.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The burger is best enjoyed immediately. If you need to store it, cool it in the refrigerator within 2 hours, wrapped in foil or plastic film. Reheat in an oven or microwave before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Grilled haddock fillet is a tender white fish meat with a subtle smoky aroma. Haddock belongs to the cod family and inhabits northern seas. Grilling preserves most nutrients while giving the dish a crisp crust.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Haddock is a staple in traditional Scandinavian and British cuisine.
Compared with cod, haddock has a firmer flesh, making it ideal for grilling.
Its omega‑3 fatty acid content is higher than that of many other marine fish.
In the wild haddock can grow up to 1.2 m, but commercial catches are usually 40–50 cm long.
The flesh turns from translucent to opaque white when cooked.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Haddock provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of omega‑3
items.content: Omega‑3 fatty acids support heart health and reduce inflammation.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The fish contains vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Haddock supplies selenium, phosphorus, and iodine, which aid thyroid function and antioxidant defense.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Unlike fattier marine fish, haddock has moderate fat content, suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to seafood, including haddock.

items.title: Heavy‑metal contamination
items.content: As with many ocean fish, haddock can accumulate mercury and other toxins; moderate consumption is advised, especially for pregnant women and children.

items.title: Overcooking
items.content: Excessive grilling can make the flesh dry and harder to digest.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Grill haddock fillets on a pre‑heated grill for 3–4 minutes per side until a golden crust forms. Season with lemon, olive oil, fresh herbs, and spices. Serve with vegetable sides, mashed potatoes, or a light salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh haddock in the refrigerator at 0–2 °C for no more than 2 days. Frozen fillets should be stored at –18 °C and used within 3–4 months. Thaw frozen fish in the fridge, not at room temperature.

content.title: About
content.content: A jelly sandwich on white bread is a simple dish made of two slices of soft white bread with sweet fruit jelly spread between them. Common jelly flavors include strawberry, cherry, and apricot. The sandwich is popular as a quick snack, breakfast item, or dessert.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first recorded mention of jelly sandwiches dates back to the 19th century in the United States.
White bread provides a neutral base that lets the jelly’s flavor shine.
In some regions the sandwich is served with butter for an added creamy note.
It is a staple in school lunches because it is easy to prepare and stays edible at room temperature for a while.
An "open-faced" version exists, where jelly is spread on a single slice of bread.

items.title: Source of quick carbs
items.content: Jelly contains simple sugars that rapidly raise blood glucose, providing a quick energy boost.

items.title: Vitamins and antioxidants
items.content: Fruit jelly is rich in vitamin C and polyphenols, which help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Some fruit jellies, such as apple, contain modest amounts of dietary fiber that aid regular bowel movements.

items.title: Mood improvement
items.content: The sweet taste can stimulate serotonin production, enhancing mood.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: The soft texture makes the sandwich easy to chew and digest, suitable for children and older adults.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Large amounts of jelly can lead to excessive sugar intake, which is detrimental to dental health and blood glucose control.

items.title: Allergy to ingredients
items.content: Some jellies may contain nuts, dairy, or preservatives that can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Gluten in bread
items.content: White bread contains gluten, making the sandwich unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Commercial jellies often contain preservatives and artificial flavors that may be undesirable with frequent consumption.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sandwich can be eaten straight away or lightly toasted to make the bread crisp and the jelly slightly melt. It is convenient to cut into bite‑size pieces for kids or serve whole slices for adults.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep a prepared sandwich in an airtight container at room temperature for no more than 4 hours. For longer storage, keep the bread and jelly separate and refrigerate each for up to 3 days.

content.title: About
content.content: White rice cooked together with a mix of vegetables is a nutritious dish enjoyed in many world cuisines. The rice provides a carbohydrate base, while the vegetables add vitamins, minerals, and fiber.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: White rice is often used as a simple side, but combined with vegetables it becomes a complete meal.
Common vegetables added include carrots, peas, corn, broccoli, and bell peppers.
The dish is traditionally steamed or simmered, preserving most of the vegetables' nutrients.
In some cultures it is served with soy sauce or spices to enhance flavor.
The recipe is easily adapted for vegetarian or vegan diets.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Rice provides a quick source of energy through its high carbohydrate content, while vegetables add slower‑digesting carbs.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Vegetables are rich in vitamin C, vitamin A, folate, and potassium, supporting immunity and skin health.

items.title: Fiber
items.content: The added vegetables increase dietary fiber, aiding digestion and promoting satiety.

items.title: Low fat
items.content: The dish contains virtually no fat, making it suitable for low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Vegetables have a high water content, helping maintain the body’s fluid balance.

items.title: Rice allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience an allergic reaction to rice.

items.title: Arsenic content
items.content: Rice from certain regions can contain elevated arsenic levels; choose reputable sources.

items.title: Glycemic index
items.content: White rice has a high glycemic index, which can cause rapid blood‑sugar spikes in people with diabetes.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot as a main course, optionally topping with sauces, spices, or proteins such as tofu, chicken, or fish. It reheats well in the microwave or on a skillet.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked rice with vegetables in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. When frozen, it can be stored for up to 2 months after cooling completely.

content.title: About
content.content: Walnuts are the edible seeds of the English walnut tree (Juglans regia), native to temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere. They have a rich, slightly bitter flavor and a crunchy texture. Walnuts are eaten raw, roasted, salted, or as walnut butter, and are used in baking, desserts, and salads.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Walnuts are among the largest tree nuts, with a hard shell surrounding the seed.
They were domesticated in Persia over 3,000 years ago.
Walnuts contain polyphenols that give them a characteristic bitter note.
In ancient cultures, walnuts symbolized wisdom and immortality.
They are a staple ingredient in Mediterranean and Asian cuisines.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Walnuts provide alpha‑linolenic acid, which supports heart and vascular health.

items.title: High in antioxidants
items.content: They contain polyphenols and vitamin E that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports brain function
items.content: The combination of polyphenols and omega‑3 may improve cognitive performance.

items.title: Contains magnesium and potassium
items.content: These minerals help regulate blood pressure and support the nervous system.

items.title: Good source of plant protein and fiber
items.content: Walnuts contribute to satiety and aid digestive health.

items.title: Tree nut allergy
items.content: Walnuts can trigger severe allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: High in calories
items.content: Because of their dense energy content, they should be consumed in moderation.

items.title: Choking hazard for children
items.content: Whole walnuts are not suitable for young children due to choking risk.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: People prone to kidney stones may need to limit intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Walnuts can be enjoyed as a snack, added to oatmeal, yogurt, salads, baked goods, or processed into walnut butter. They are often roasted lightly with a pinch of salt to enhance flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store walnuts in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent oil oxidation. Discard any nuts that smell rancid.
